entry.title: The winter California turned into a lake 🌊

media:group.media:title: The winter California turned into a lake 🌊
media:group.media:description:
Could a storm like 1862 hit California again? 👇
In the winter of 1861–62, about 43 days of storms filled the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys into an inland sea about 300 miles long. Governor Leland Stanford rowed to his inauguration, at least 4,000 people died, and the USGS ARkStorm scenario estimates a repeat today would cost about $725 billion.
Sources: USGS ("ARkStorm Scenario", "ARkStorm: California's Other 'Big One'"), William H. Brewer, "Up and Down California in 1860–1864", Wikipedia ("Great Flood of 1862")
Images (Wikimedia Commons): • Cumulus clouds in fair weather.jpeg — Michael Jastremski, CC BY-SA 2.0
Footage and images: NASA (images.nasa.gov)

entry.title: Why 87°F can be too hot for your body 🥵

media:group.media:title: Why 87°F can be too hot for your body 🥵
media:group.media:description:
What's the most humid place you've ever been? 👇
Your body cools itself by evaporating sweat, and very humid air stops that. In a 2022 Penn State HEAT Project study, 24 young adults lost control of their core temperature at a wet-bulb temperature of about 31°C (87°F at 100% humidity), well below the 35°C limit long assumed.
Sources: Penn State News ("Humans can't endure temperatures and humidities as high as previously thought", 2022), Penn State Institutes of Energy and the Environment ("Beyond the thermometer"), Vecellio et al., Journal of Applied Physiology (PSU HEAT Project), AAAS / Raymond et al., Science Advances (2020)
Footage and images: NASA (images.nasa.gov)
#Shorts #heatwave #humanbody #science #facts

entry.title: What if asteroid Apophis hit Earth in 2029? ☄️

media:group.media:title: What if asteroid Apophis hit Earth in 2029? ☄️
media:group.media:description:
Would you go outside to watch it pass? 👇
Asteroid Apophis, 1,115 feet wide, will pass about 20,000 miles above Earth on April 13, 2029, closer than geosynchronous satellites. Early estimates gave it a 2.7% chance of impact; 2021 radar observations ruled out any impact for at least 100 years.
Sources: NASA ("Apophis Facts"), NASA JPL ("NASA Analysis: Earth Is Safe From Asteroid Apophis for 100-Plus Years", 2021), The Planetary Society ("Will Apophis hit Earth?")
Footage and images: NASA (images.nasa.gov)
#Shorts #apophis #asteroid #space #whatif #science #facts

entry.title: The afternoon a wall of dirt blacked out Kansas 🌪️

media:group.media:title: The afternoon a wall of dirt blacked out Kansas 🌪️
media:group.media:description:
Could a storm like Black Sunday happen again today? 👇
On April 14, 1935, a dust cloud up to 600 feet tall hit Dodge City, Kansas, at 50 to 60 mph and turned afternoon into night across the Great Plains. It was the worst of the Dust Bowl storms that pushed about 3.5 million people off the Plains.
Sources: National Weather Service Dodge City ("Black Sunday 1935"), National Weather Service Norman ("April 14, 1935 Black Sunday"), UT Austin EarthDate ("Dust Bowl 2"), Wikipedia ("Dust Bowl", "Black Sunday (storm)")
#Shorts #dustbowl #history #weather #mystery #darkhistory

entry.title: What a year in space did to Scott Kelly's body 🚀

media:group.media:title: What a year in space did to Scott Kelly's body 🚀
media:group.media:description:
Would you spend a year in space for this? 👇
NASA's Twins Study compared astronaut Scott Kelly, after 340 days on the International Space Station, with his identical twin Mark on Earth. His spine stretched, his telomeres lengthened and then shortened within 48 hours of landing, and about 91% of his gene expression changes returned to baseline.
Sources: NASA ("NASA's Twins Study Results Published in Science", 2019), The Physiological Society / Vernice, Bailey & Mason ("Telomeres and genomic instability during long-duration spaceflight"), Spaceflight Now ("Kelly describes re-adaptation to gravity", 2016)
Footage and images: NASA (images.nasa.gov)
#Shorts #space #astronaut #humanbody #science #facts

entry.title: The Carroll A. Deering: Where Did the Ghost Ship's 11 Men Go?

media:group.media:title: The Carroll A. Deering: Where Did the Ghost Ship's 11 Men Go?
media:group.media:description:
Mutiny, pirates or something else: what do you think happened to the crew? 👇
In January 1921, a five-masted schooner ran aground on Diamond Shoals off Cape Hatteras with her sails set, her lights burning and food in the galley. Her eleven men were gone. This case file follows the mate's threat in Barbados, the last sighting at the Cape Lookout lightship, the faked bottle message and the federal investigation that never closed the case.
Sources: U.S. National Archives, Herbert Hoover Presidential Library ("The Wreck of the Carroll A. Deering"); U.S. Coast Guard ("Ghostship Carroll A. Deering"); National Park Service, Cape Hatteras National Seashore; North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources; Wikipedia, "Carroll A. Deering" and its references.

entry.title: What if Earth's magnetic field switched off? 🧲

media:group.media:title: What if Earth's magnetic field switched off? 🧲
media:group.media:description:
Would you rather lose the magnetic field or the ozone layer? 👇
What would happen if Earth's magnetic field disappeared? 41,000 years ago, during the Laschamp event, it fell to about 5% of today's strength. Mars shows what a planet without a global field looks like over billions of years.
Sources: University of Oulu / Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics (Laschamp excursion, 2026), University of Michigan via Space.com ("41,000 years ago, auroras blazed near the equator"), NASA MAVEN mission (Spaceflight Now, 2015), Wikipedia ("South Atlantic Anomaly")
Footage and images: NASA (images.nasa.gov)

entry.title: The earthquake wave that crossed the Pacific 🌊

media:group.media:title: The earthquake wave that crossed the Pacific 🌊
media:group.media:description:
Could a tsunami warning today stop this from happening again? 👇
On May 22, 1960, a magnitude 9.5 earthquake in southern Chile, the strongest ever recorded, sent a tsunami across the whole Pacific. It hit Hilo, Hawaii, about 15 hours later and Japan about 22 hours later, where nobody had felt the quake and no alert was issued.
Sources: Britannica ("Chile earthquake of 1960"), INGV Centro Allerta Tsunami ("22 May 1960: sixty years after the biggest earthquake ever recorded and the global tsunami"), USGS

entry.title: How long you'd last if your plane lost pressure ✈️

media:group.media:title: How long you'd last if your plane lost pressure ✈️
media:group.media:description:
Would you get your mask on in time? 👇
What happens to your body if a plane loses cabin pressure at 35,000 feet? Aviation medicine tables give you 30 seconds to 1 minute of useful consciousness, and low oxygen can feel calm, even pleasant. In FAA altitude chamber tests, people couldn't write their names but thought they were fine.
Sources: FAA ("Hypoxia: The Higher You Fly… The Less Air in the Sky"), Naval Medical Research Unit Dayton (NAMRU-D Report 16-19, time of useful consciousness table), Wikipedia ("Helios Airways Flight 522", citing the Greek AAIASB final report)

Footage and images: NASA (images.nasa.gov)

entry.title: What would happen if you stood on Venus? 🔥

media:group.media:title: What would happen if you stood on Venus? 🔥
media:group.media:description:
Would you rather try Venus or Mars? 👇
What would happen to you on the surface of Venus? The air pressure is about 92 times Earth's, the ground is about 860°F, and the Soviet lander Venera 13 lasted just 127 minutes there in 1982. NASA's Parker Solar Probe even caught the rock glowing through the clouds.
Sources: The Planetary Society ("What would it be like to stand on the surface of Venus?"), NASA / AGU ("First visible light images of Venus' surface from space captured by Parker Solar Probe", 2022), Guinness World Records ("Longest time survived on Venus by a spacecraft")
Footage and images: NASA (images.nasa.gov)
#Shorts #venus #space #nasa #whatif #science #facts

entry.title: The day the Mississippi River ran backward 🌊

media:group.media:title: The day the Mississippi River ran backward 🌊
media:group.media:description:
Could this happen in the middle of America again? 👇
In the winter of 1811–1812, three magnitude 7+ earthquakes hit the New Madrid area of Missouri and Arkansas. Witnesses saw the Mississippi flow upstream, the river briefly got waterfalls, and the ground sank into what is now Reelfoot Lake.
Sources: USGS ("Summary of 1811-1812 New Madrid Earthquakes Sequence"), Wikipedia ("1811–1812 New Madrid earthquakes", eyewitness account of Eliza Bryan, 1816), UC Santa Barbara Geography

entry.title: How many G's can your body take? 🚀

media:group.media:title: How many G's can your body take? 🚀
media:group.media:description:
Have you ever felt your vision fade on a ride or a fast stand-up? 👇
Why do pilots black out under G-force, and how much can a human survive? Centrifuge studies show blackout starting around 4 to 5.6 G, while Air Force doctor John Stapp survived 46.2 G on a rocket sled in 1954.
Sources: NIH / StatPearls ("G-Force Induced Loss of Consciousness"), Wikipedia ("John Stapp", citing Aviation Week, 1955), NASA
Footage and images: NASA (images.nasa.gov)
#Shorts #gforce #pilot #humanbody #science #facts

entry.title: The Dyatlov Pass Incident: Why Did 9 Hikers Run Into the Snow?

media:group.media:title: The Dyatlov Pass Incident: Why Did 9 Hikers Run Into the Snow?
media:group.media:description:
What do you think drove them out of the tent? 👇
In February 1959, nine experienced hikers left their tent on a frozen slope in the northern Ural Mountains, in the middle of the night, without their boots. This case file follows the search, the investigation, the theories and the 2021 avalanche study that finally offered an answer — and the questions it still leaves open.
Sources: Communications Earth & Environment (Gaume & Puzrin, 2021); EPFL; Wikipedia, "Dyatlov Pass incident" and its references.

entry.title: What if you fell into Jupiter? 🪐

media:group.media:title: What if you fell into Jupiter? 🪐
media:group.media:description:
How far down do you think you'd get? 👇
Jupiter has no solid surface. NASA's Galileo probe dropped into it in 1995 at 106,000 mph and lasted 58 minutes before the pressure and heat silenced it. Here's what that fall would do to you.
Sources: NASA Science ("Jupiter Facts"), NASA Science ("Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe"), NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory

entry.title: The year the Sun turned blood red over Europe 🌋

media:group.media:title: The year the Sun turned blood red over Europe 🌋
media:group.media:description:
Could a volcano do this again today? 👇
In 1783, Iceland's Laki fissure erupted for about 8 months. Its sulfur haze spread over most of Europe and as far as Syria, the Sun looked blood red at sunrise and sunset, and the Haze Famine that followed killed about one-fifth of Iceland's people.
Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica ("Laki"), Encyclopédie de l'environnement ("The Laki Fissure eruption, 1783-1784"), Scientific American ("How the Laki eruptions changed history")
#Shorts #volcano #iceland #history #mystery #darkhistory
